title: Christ, the Yes to God’s Promises
english: …obscure, but rather simple and true, saying, “Our word to you was not yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:18). That is, he was not at war with himself or sick with inconsistency, praising a thing at one time and blaming it at another, but he spoke the truth in his preaching. So “God is faithful” (2 Corinthians 1:18), that is, free of falsehood and true.

The learned men of the Greeks will hold differing opinions about the gods they believe in, saying both yes and no; for truth is not among them, but rather falsehood. That is why they are tossed about by differing opinions. But He who is truly and by nature the Son of God Almighty, how could He become yes and no? …

Necessarily, then, the Son who is from Him by nature, “who was proclaimed among you by us, by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:19). For every word about Him spoken through the voice of those who spoke for God has proved true. And “as many as are the promises of God,” he says, “in Him is the Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20); that is, in Him we have received from God the Father every bounty and every promise. And this is “in the Yes,” that is, in truth; for these things have come to their fulfillment through Christ. For “death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), the power of corruption has been overthrown, and weakness too will cease, and dishonor besides (1 Corinthians 15:43), just as the most wise Paul also said in his first letter.

We have also been declared heirs and sharers of the very kingdom of the saints. For He in whom is the Yes will Himself say to us at the divine judgment seat, “Come, you blessed of My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). By nature we are servants; but through Him we have been called from slavery to the dignity of the free, from corruption to incorruption, and we have been set free from serving the devil.

Every promise of God through Christ, then, has the Yes alone; the No, which is denial, is altogether inadmissible, for He Himself is the Truth (John 14:6). From this he also shows, of this One in particular, that He is God by nature. For if He would not break the promises, but will rather bring them to fulfillment for the saints, though it is God the Father who distributes the good things, how could He not be Son by nature and in truth, and God from God, He in whom, without falsehood, is “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James 1:17)?

That the word is free of falsehood he confirms further, saying, “Therefore through Him also is the Amen to God, for glory through us” (2 Corinthians 1:20). For since He is the Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), through whom alone the Father can be approached, and in whom is every spiritual gift, surely through Him every prayer will also reach its fulfillment; and this is the Amen. The Son Himself has taught us this, saying to the holy apostles, “In that day you will ask Me nothing. Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything, He will give it to you in My name. Until now you have asked nothing in My name; ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16:23–24). Through Him, then, is the Amen to God the Father, for glory through us. For it is our custom to close every prayer in the name of Christ.

That He Himself would not lack the glory that befits Him we shall see without effort, when the blessed Jacob prophesies, “Judah, may your brothers praise you” (Genesis 49:8), for Christ sprang from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14); and when the prophet Isaiah says, “I saw the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1), with the seraphim standing around Him, calling Him holy, naming Him Lord of hosts, and saying that heaven and earth are full of His glory (Isaiah 6:2–3). And that it was the Son Himself whom he beheld, the wise John will show when he says, “Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory …
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: the first words finish the last sentence of the previous section (“his word had not been double and … obscure”). Cyril is speaking of Paul's preaching, “our word to you” (2 Corinthians 1:18), not of Christ the Word.

title: The Father Establishes and Seals Us in Christ
english: … and spoke about Him” (John 12:41). So even if the Father is glorified through Him, and since He has been set forth as “a propitiation through faith” (Romans 3:25), and has also become “a minister of the holy places” (Hebrews 8:2) because of His humanity, offering as a priest the prayer of each of the saints as a spiritual sacrifice (for through Him is our Amen), still He could not be thought to stand outside the duty of being worshiped and glorified together with the One who begot Him, both by us and by the multitude of holy spirits above.

The inspired Paul says somewhere, “And when He again brings the Firstborn into the world, He says, ‘Let all the angels of God worship Him’” (Hebrews 1:6). And yet to which of all beings is it unclear that He is Only-begotten insofar as He is understood to be God? For He alone has been begotten of the Father alone. But when He lowered Himself into our condition and came to be among many brothers (Romans 8:29), then He was set in the first place. So besides being Only-begotten as God, He has also been called Firstborn because of His humanity.

“Now He who establishes us with you in Christ,” and so on (2 Corinthians 1:21). God the Father establishes us in Christ by setting a right and unshaken faith in the souls of all, persuading them to hold that He is God by nature and in truth, even if He was seen in our form, He who is above all creation having been born of a woman according to the flesh. Indeed, when Peter confessed the faith and said plainly, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), our Lord Jesus Christ Himself answered, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but My Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). For since the mystery is exceedingly great, it would rightly need instruction from above, from the Father. So it is God Himself, who has also sealed us and anointed us and given us the pledge of the Spirit, who establishes us in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).

From these words too it should be clear to us that the Son did not become “yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:19), but is rather true God, and that in all good things “in Him is the Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20). For while God is said to seal and anoint us and to have given the pledge of the Spirit, it is again Christ who accomplishes these things in us, not as a servant, nor anointing and sealing us with a Spirit foreign to Him, but with the very Spirit that is His own and the Father’s. For the Holy Spirit is in both, because of the sameness of substance, not divided, but as reaching from the Father through the Son to the creation. For He breathed on the holy apostles, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

Through Him and in Him we have been sealed into the divine and spiritual image. For the divine apostle himself, writing to the Galatians, said, “My little children, for whom I am again in the pains of birth until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). And if, by being formed into Christ, we gain the riches of the divine image in ourselves, then He Himself is the image of God the Father and His exact likeness, not as we are, called to likeness by sharing in holiness, but rather by nature and in substance. For He who is God by nature can have nothing unlike Himself in the One who is God by nature and in truth and begotten of His own substance.

The most wise John says that He too has been sealed by God the Father: “For whoever has received His testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true” (John 3:33). Yet He has been sealed, again, not in the same way as we are, but with the Father all but writing His whole self into the nature of the Son and, as it were, imprinting Himself there in substance. That is why He said, “Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).
“But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us makes known the fragrance of the knowledge of Him in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:14). The apostles give thanks …

“The Spirit that is His own and the Father's”: Cyril holds that the Son gives the Spirit as His own, not as a servant handing on another's gift.
“And so on” renders κ.τ.λ., by which Cyril cuts short the verse he is quoting.

title: Christ as the Fragrance of the Knowledge of God
english: … as they are tested and toil, and they glory in the struggles they endure for Christ. For just as Christ was put on display for our sake when He endured death on the tree and was made perfect through sufferings (Hebrews 2:10), so they too say that they are led in triumph for Him, that is, made known to people everywhere and made glorious through trials, and that they conquer the world by being ready to suffer all things, and very gladly, for the name of Christ. For they are sharers in His sufferings and, as he says, partakers “of the glory that is to be revealed” (1 Peter 5:1).

They say that it is God who leads them in triumph, not as handing them over to suffering, nor as heaping afflictions on them, but because, by His good pleasure, as they proclaim Jesus to people throughout the whole world under heaven, they fall into the trials that come for His sake. For without trials it is impossible to win approval. And the fruit of these trials is that they suffer in Christ, that is, for Christ’s sake, which is glorious and full of good hopes.

What, then, is this fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father, made known to the world through the holy apostles, and in every place, as they themselves say? The inspired Paul himself will teach us again when he says, “For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5); and again, “For I decided to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and Him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).

How, then, will He who was born of a woman, who endured the cross and underwent death, even though He came to life again, be the fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father, if, as some suppose, Christ is thought to be a mere man like us, that is, a God-bearing man, and not Himself God by nature, even if the Word from God is understood to have taken up the human in the plan of salvation? For by being like us and nothing more, He will not give forth the fragrance of the nature of God the Father; nor would He who endured death become the fragrance of the One who knows no death.

How, then, is Christ the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father? Is it not clear that it is insofar as He is understood to be God, and is God, even though He appeared in the flesh for our sake? Otherwise, how do those who preach Christ proclaim to the world the One who is God by nature and in truth? Or how could they know Jesus? And how is God the Father said by the holy teachers of the mysteries to be reconciling the world to Himself in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19), unless one accepts the humanity into union with the Word who was born of God, as the wise plan of salvation required? For the inspired disciples, speaking in the Spirit, proclaim the Word of God not as having dwelt in a man, but as having become flesh (John 1:14), that is, as united to flesh that has a rational soul. For in this way the One who was crucified would also be the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8).

So whether the Word from God is thought of with the flesh, or not so, but by Himself, as before He became like us, He is the fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father, since in His own nature He spreads to us the fragrance of the One from whom He is. And if what I say is true, how could He be something that came into being, counted among those who received their being out of nothing? For such a one could not become the fragrance of the One who is uncreated and who does not exist as something brought into being. For we shall not see what has come into being in what never came into being, nor what never came into being in what has come into being.

Yet the Son has shown the Father in Himself; therefore He is God by nature, because of the sameness of substance. So let the Son hear from us as well, “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song of Songs 1:3); for through Him and in Him we have come to know the God and Father from whom He was begotten.
“For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Corinthians 2:15).
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: the first words continue “The apostles give thanks …” from the end of the previous section.
“A God-bearing man” (θεοφόρος ἄνθρωπος) is the view Cyril rejects: that Christ was a man who carried God within him, not God made man.
The phrase about the glory to be revealed is the wording of 1 Peter 5:1; compare Romans 8:17–18.
The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 328–329) are left out of the text; one of them falls inside the word ἐσταυρωμένος (“crucified”), which is read whole.
